blocks.content: Vertical stratification in a forest maximizes light capture and creates distinct ecological niches across varying heights.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Vertical stratification is the structural arrangement of forest vegetation into distinct horizontal layers driven by light gradient.
The Emergent Layer consists of giant trees towering above the forest crown, exposed to strong winds and intense solar radiation.
The Canopy Layer forms a continuous umbrella-like roof where the highest biodiversity and photosynthetic activity occur.
The Understory Layer receives limited filtered sunlight and is dominated by shade-tolerant shrubs, saplings, and epiphytes.
The Forest Floor is characterized by high humidity, low light (<2%), and rapid decomposition of organic matter by soil organisms.

rows: Giant trees, eagles, bats, broad-winged birds
Dense tree crowns, arboreal mammals, birds, epiphytes
Fungi, decomposers, insects, fallen leaf litter

items: Sequence of layers from top to bottom: Emergent Layer -> Canopy -> Understory -> Forest Floor.
Canopy layer houses over 50% of all forest plant and animal species due to maximum productivity.
Light intensity decreases exponentially from the canopy to the forest floor, driving physiological adaptations in understory vegetation.
